description:
We are a team of two, united by our curiosity about space, astronomy and the possibilities of technology. The fascination of understanding distant celestial objects through observations collected from Earth has always motivated us to explore more and learn how the universe is studied.

Together, we worked towards a shared vision of making real astronomical observations more engaging to explore, easier to understand and meaningful to a wider audience.
summary:
Skies Through Time is an interactive astronomical exploration platform built around real observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. It connects the visual wonder of space with the discoveries hidden within scientific data, creating an immersive, public-facing experience through direct, hands-on astronomical exploration.

SPHEREx surveys the entire sky in 102 infrared spectral channels, spanning wavelengths from 0.75 to 5 micrometres. Skies Through Time helps people explore the information gathered through this mission and understand what it can reveal.

How It Addresses the Challenge:-
As space missions collect enormous amounts of astronomical data, making those observations meaningful to a wider audience is just as important as collecting them. Although mission archives contain valuable information, understanding scientific data can be challenging without an astronomical background. Skies Through Time bridges this gap by turning mission observations into an engaging, educational experience that brings real research closer to students, space enthusiasts and the public.

Why Is It Important:-
Many people are fascinated by space but rarely get to understand how we observe and study it. Skies Through Time turns that curiosity into exploration, helping users understand infrared astronomy, telescope observations and the changing universe through real mission data and guided exploration.
details:
What Our Project Does and How It Works:

Skies Through Time turns SPHEREx observations into an interactive journey through the sky. Through Sky Explorer, users can navigate the celestial map, search for objects by name or coordinates, and select regions to retrieve actual observations from NASA's archive. Each selected region comes with an observation history showing when and how frequently SPHEREx has surveyed that part of the sky.

The platform offers several ways to investigate these observations. Time-Lapse Sky plays images from different dates in sequence, making changes in an object's position or brightness easier to notice. Infrared Explorer lets users examine the same region across SPHEREx's 102 infrared spectral channels, spanning 0.75 to 5 micrometres. Spectrum Explorer provides a quick-look graph of an object's brightness across these wavelengths.

For deeper investigation, Before & After aligns observations from two different dates and generates a difference image to highlight changes. Change Finder examines successive observations to identify significant variations. Object Tracker follows potential moving sources across multiple visits, estimates their motion and records their measured positions. Building on this, Future Position projects where a tracked source may appear based on its observed movement.

The experience also connects with external astronomical resources. Star Catalogue Overlay displays known stars in the selected region, while Cross-Observatory Search finds observations of the same region from facilities and archives including Hubble, JWST, Gemini and NEOSSat through CADC. Users can save interesting objects, predictions and personal observations using Discovery Journal and Watchlist.

Benefits of the Project:

  • A gateway to real astronomical research: Users can interact with actual mission observations and explore the information behind them, bringing scientific data closer to people who may never have worked with astronomical archives.
  • A deeper understanding of how we observe the universe: The platform helps users understand that astronomical images are scientific measurements, not simply photographs of distant planets and stars. Exploring infrared channels and spectra introduces them to how telescopes collect information that our eyes cannot see.
  • Learning through exploration: Instead of encountering astronomy only through textbooks or explanations, students can investigate real observations, experiment with different wavelengths and discover how astronomical changes are studied.
  • A broader view of individual discoveries: Connecting SPHEREx observations with Gaia, NEOSSat and other observatory archives gives users additional context about the objects and regions they explore.
  • An ongoing space for curiosity: With saved objects, predictions and personal notes, users can build on their discoveries instead of treating each exploration as a one-time experience.

Intended Impact:

We want to make astronomical exploration something more people can participate in, not just something they admire from a distance. A student exploring a region of the sky should be able to move beyond asking what an object looks like and begin asking how it was observed, what its infrared measurements reveal and whether anything about it has changed.

We also hope to create a stronger connection between public curiosity and scientific thinking. Understanding how space telescopes collect observations, why different wavelengths matter and how astronomers interpret changes can help people appreciate the work behind every scientific discovery.

In the long term, we envision Skies Through Time growing into a richer public-facing space exploration platform, incorporating more astronomical datasets and deeper scientific capabilities. Our ambition is to make exploring the universe a starting point for learning, questioning and discovering.

Tools We Used:

  • Frontend: React and Three.js for the interactive celestial interface and 3D visual elements.
  • Backend and API: Python 3.13 and FastAPI, with Uvicorn serving the application and connecting frontend requests to backend processing.
  • Astronomical Processing: Astropy, NumPy and SciPy for astronomical data handling and scientific computations.
  • Data Validation: Pydantic for validating and structuring application data.
  • Database: SQLAlchemy and SQLite for local data storage, including the Discovery Journal.
  • Caching: Redis for temporary caching of retrieved astronomical data and images.
  • Hosting: Vercel is being considered for deployment.

What Makes Our Project Creative:

We wanted the experience of exploring space to feel closer to actually being among the stars. Rather than presenting astronomy as a collection of charts, tables and isolated images, Skies Through Time places users inside an immersive celestial environment. A galaxy-inspired background, a field of stars and selectable celestial objects create the feeling of floating through space, where every point can lead to something worth discovering.

But the visual experience is only the beginning. What makes the concept meaningful is the connection between that sense of wonder and the science behind it. When someone selects a distant object, they are not simply opening a photograph of it. They are accessing observations collected by a space telescope, measurements across infrared wavelengths and information that can help explain how astronomers study that region. Space telescopes collect light and scientific measurements, often beyond the range of human vision, which scientists process and interpret to understand the universe.

We want users to experience that process in a way that feels natural. They can begin with the beauty of the sky, follow their curiosity into actual observations and gradually discover the science behind what they are seeing. By bringing immersive exploration, real astronomical data and investigative tools together, Skies Through Time connects the emotional appeal of space with the excitement of scientific discovery.

Factors Our Team Considered:

  • Scientific accuracy: We work with actual SPHEREx observations and preserve the distinction between astronomical measurements, visual representations and quick-look analysis.
  • Ease of exploration: The interface is designed to make complex astronomical information easier to navigate without removing its scientific context.
  • Data handling: Telescope images are retrieved on demand rather than permanently stored by the platform, with temporary caching used to support repeated access.
  • Performance: As astronomical datasets can be large, the system retrieves relevant observations for the selected sky region rather than attempting to load the entire survey at once.
  • Responsible interpretation: Automated detections and predicted positions are presented as potential findings and estimates, not confirmed discoveries. The spectrum feature is also identified as a quick-look analysis rather than a replacement for professional scientific processing.
